newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians pray for peace, protest at settlement.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians pray for peace, protest at settlement.

text.p: Under heavy Israeli security, Moslem and Christian Palestinians prayed for peace during a demonstration on Friday against Israeli plans to build a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

Soldiers of Israel's Givati infantry brigade in battle gear -- backed by snipers and at least one machinegun -- took up positions on a hill overlooking the demonstration, as some 3,000 Palestinians and Israeli peace activists marched with placards and Palestinian flags from the town of Beit Sahour.
"We, the sons of this land, gathered here with one heart... to pray for peace," the Rev. Yaacoub Abu Saada, head of the Malakite church in Bethlehem, said in a speech after the prayers.

Tension rose briefly when some young demonstrators climbed up the hill near the soldiers. But protest organisers defused the tension by standing between the two sides. The demonstration ended peacefully.

"This is our land. They want to take it and build a settlement. Our village, Um Touba, has been here for 1,000 years and now they want to bring us people from Russia and Ethiopia to live here instead of us," said Hussein Abu Tair, a village leader, referring to Israelis who immigrated from the two countries.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu enraged Palestinians on February 26 when his government approved a plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews at Jabal Abu Ghneim in East Jerusalem. Israel calls the site Har Homa.

Palestinians had called for a demonstration of 10,000 people on the site on Friday. But organisers said Israeli military checkpoints erected on roads leading to the site on the southern edge of Jerusalem barred many from joining the protest.
Israeli security forces deployed 2,500 policemen and soldiers throughout East and at Jabal Abu Ghneim, a hill of pine trees, to prevent any possible violence.
"We have information that there is tension in the air," newly appointed Jerusalem police chief Yair Yitzhaki told Israel Radio.
A team of Palestinian organisers wearing green baseball hats placed themselves between demonstrators and the Israeli forces, who formed a line opposite the protesters.

"We came out today in this peaceful demonstration, but those who decide the outcome are those soldiers and the orders that were given to them," Faisal al-Husseini, the top PLO official in Jerusalem, told the demonstrators through a loudspeaker.
Palestinian Authority Minister Elias Freij, the mayor of Bethlehem which is just south of Har Homa, called on Netanyahu to stop settlement and pursue peace.
"I tell Mr Netanyahu Jews and Palestinians are destined by God to live in this country together and forever," Freij said.
"So which is best: to live in peace as good neighbours or to remain as enemies quarrelling, fighting and shouting and suffering and screaming?"

Israel further enraged Palestinians on Friday when it announced that it was handing back only two percent of some 70 percent of West Bank land still under its exclusive control to the PLO under a self-rule deal.
Under a proposal narrowly approved by Israel's cabinet overnight, another seven percent of the West Bank would be transferred from joint Israel-PLO rule to Palestinian control.

About 50 Palestinians youths hurled stones on Friday at two Israeli border police jeeps that entered the West Bank village of Beit Ummar, which according to press reports would be included in the further redeployment, witnesses said.
The Israelis parked at the entrance of the village but did not respond to the stone-throwers.
